articles.title: Is it true that … you need to take 10,000 steps a day to be healthy?
articles.summary: The fitness benchmark has surprisingly unscientific origins – yet it does contain more than a kernel of truth. The idea that we need to walk 10,000 steps a day originated not in medical research but in a 1960s marketing campaign for a pedometer, says Jack McNamara, senior lecturer in clinical…
body: “When the research community looked into it, they found that there were health benefits, so it didn’t necessarily get thrown out as pseudoscience,” says McNamara.

Walking has been shown to benefit cardiovascular and cardiorespiratory health, as well as reducing the likelihood of some cancers. It also breaks up sedentary time, which is hugely harmful to health. “But when we look into it with systematic reviews and large-scale studies, there start to be diminishing returns the more steps you do.”

McNamara says the health improvement is huge when someone goes from a sedentary lifestyle, or 2,000 steps a day to 4,000. But going from 8,000 to 10,000 or 10,000 to 12,000 brings a much smaller benefit. “It still has some benefits, just not as many as people might expect.”

That’s not to say we should spend more time sitting down. If you enjoy walking, McNamara says, walk for as long as you like. The problem comes when you start chasing step counts for their own sake, particularly if you punish yourself for missing them.
points: The fitness benchmark has surprisingly unscientific origins – yet it does contain more than a kernel of truth.

articles.title: A perfect weekend in the Lincolnshire Wolds: wide skies and gentle walks
articles.summary: The landscape of rolling hills and chalk valleys that inspired Tennyson is the perfect setting for an autumnal short break. Here’s where to eat, where to stay and what not to miss.
body: The Lincolnshire Wolds National Landscape covers an area of 216 sq miles. On its southern boundary, halfway between Lincoln and the coast, the friendly market town of Horncastle bills itself as the “gateway to the Wolds”. With handsome brick houses, great cafes, a market on Thursdays and Saturdays and decent public transport links, it’s a perfect base for exploring the area.

Horncastle overflows with antique shops. Laurence Shaw, with half a century’s knowledge of the trade, runs an elegant wholesaler on the corner of East Street. In an old chapel across the road, the Trinity Centre has all kinds of ancient treasures piled in fantastical heaps under lancets of Victorian glass: porcelain milkmaids, jelly moulds, cotton reels, teetering piles of teacups and thick vines of jewellery. Round the corner in Stanhope Antique Centre you may find anything from a wooden decoy duck to a roulette wheel between chandeliers and grandfather clocks.
points: The landscape of rolling hills and chalk valleys that inspired Tennyson is the perfect setting for an autumnal short break.

articles.title: The one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private life
articles.summary: I’d become obsessed with appealing to my invisible audience. But since I ditched the app a year ago, my quieter moments have taken on brilliant new meaning. I first downloaded Instagram when I was 17 and became hooked on it the way most people fall in love: slowly, and then all at once.
body: As I went through my university years, however, certain changes crept up on me. I began to swap reading – or essay-writing – for hours spent curating new posts. On my way home from lectures (or later, from my work as a journalist), I would spend ages trying to take the artsiest, most perfect picture of that evening’s sunset for my story – as if the people who followed me were eagerly awaiting yet another photo of one of the Earth’s rotations. What usually followed was a night of reloading my feed to see how many people had reacted to my post – or worse, hadn’t reacted at all.

It wasn’t until a trip to Sri Lanka last year that I realised how far my obsession had gone. My partner and I spent two weeks travelling through Negombo and Kandy, having dinner in front of the Indian Ocean and visiting ancient heritage sites that I will probably never see again.
points: I’d become obsessed with appealing to my invisible audience.

articles.title: Spaghetti with lentils, and aubergine veggie-balls: Jacob Kenedy’s autumn pasta recipes
articles.summary: A deliciously humble lentil and spaghetti dish, and a meat-free riff on meatball pasta made with aubergine veggie-balls. Some plant-based pasta dishes are light, bright and summery – pesto genovese, tomato sauce, aglio e olio – but some have an umami and complexity that is normally associated with…
body: As I write this, my mum is just as alive and at least as vital as she was when she used to make this dish for me, but, for some reason, this is now a dish I make more often, and for her. I adore it, but every time I have offered it to an Italian they look at me as though I have just insulted their mother. Don’t ask me why; people can be as inexplicable as this dish is delicious. You can add some chilli (dried or fresh) when you fry the garlic, if you like, but I prefer this comfortingly bland and without pep.
Cook the pasta according to packet instructions in abundant, well-salted water (10g per litre).
Meanwhile, fry the garlic in a saucepan in half the oil over a medium heat until golden, no darker. Add the lentils and a splash of pasta water, then bring to the boil.

articles.title: Sheer Looks to Lingerie: Are GLP-1s Changing the Way We Dress?
articles.summary: With sheer fabrics, lingerie, and skin-revealing cutouts and lace, SS27’s biggest trends put the body front and center. As GLP-1 and weight loss medications dominate global conversations, is it mere coincidence or a signal of a broader shift?
body: Bullet bras and high-cut briefs at Tom Ford. Corsets and garter skirts at Balmain. Skirts-as-belts at Ashlyn. And sheer organza on almost every runway. These are just some of the lingerie-inspired, transparent or cinched pieces that flooded show collections this Spring/Summer 2027 season. But beyond the cyclical nature of sex appeal and its revolving role within fashion, this surge of skin brings something deeper into focus at a time plagued by shrinking bodies: the relationship between GLP-1s and the runway.

The conversation around weight loss medications such as GLP-1s can, at times, feel ubiquitous. GLP-1 sales hit $79 billion in 2025, per Morgan Stanley Research, and the global market is projected to reach $190 billion by 2035. A June 2026 report from the Consumer Goods Forum and Bain & Co. forecasts the use of GLP-1s to reach one in three Americans and one in eight Britons by 2030.
points: With sheer fabrics, lingerie, and skin-revealing cutouts and lace, SS27’s biggest trends put the body front and center.

articles.title: The Vogue Business Spring/Summer 2027 Size Inclusivity Report
articles.summary: Amid accelerating access to GLP-1s, conservative undercurrents and a few glimmers of hope, curve representation on the runway remains low at just 2.5%.
body: This season, only a handful of household names featured mid or plus-size models in their shows, including McQueen, Ferragamo, and Miu Miu. These bright spots in an otherwise barren season for curve representation weren’t necessarily novel. Big designers have done this on several occasions in recent years, although it’s never extended beyond the occasional deployment of larger models.

The Spring/Summer 2027 schedule was an urgent confirmation of how badly the industry has regressed since FW23, when Vogue Business began tracking size inclusivity on the runway. Following some seasons of incremental growth between FW23 and SS25, total curve representation has regressed or plateaued season after season, between 2-3%.

articles.title: “We Are Facing a Pandemic of People Shrinking”: 3 Designers on the State of Size Inclusivity
articles.summary: As the rest of the industry regresses when it comes to size inclusivity, some designers are holding firm. But at what cost?
body: As fashion keeps getting skinnier, there are a few designers who are still fighting the good fight. When size-inclusive designers Ester Manas, Sinéad O’Dwyer or Karoline Vitto don’t show in Paris or London, respectively, the city’s mid and plus-size representation plummets, according to four years of Vogue Business Size Inclusivity reports.
A look from Karoline Vitto’s LFW FW26 collection. She showed in her native Brazil for SS27 at Rio Fashion Week.

While established brands show the occasional curve look on the catwalk (typically on the back of one of few famous curve models), the aforementioned designers commit to size inclusivity season after season. And they don’t just present bigger bodies on the catwalk. They actually design, produce and sell mid and plus-size clothing, and are building small but hyper-engaged communities of customers who are thrilled to be able to wear creative but well-fitting luxury clothes.
points: As the rest of the industry regresses when it comes to size inclusivity, some designers are holding firm.

articles.title: An Exclusive Behind-the-Scenes Look at the 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show
articles.summary: Corey Tenold photographs the best behind-the-scenes moments at the 2026 Victoria's Secret Fashion Show.
body: The Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show is back, yet again, this time with its “angels” touching down on the West Coast. This year’s blowout takes place on the Sony lot in Los Angeles, where a lineup of A-list models (Gigi Hadid, Paloma Elsesser, Adriana Lima, Candice Swanepoel, Ashley Graham, Joan Smalls, and many more) traipsed the length of the runway between bookings from au courant pop stars that prove the brand’s cultural (and financial) might: Tate McCray, KATSEYE, Megan Moroney, and Megan Thee Stallion included. And, of course, the return of the brand’s much-ballyhooed Fantasy Bra, a curve-hugging piece of lingerie that is loaded up with diamonds and revealed on a VIP model.
